name: Blues

tagline.text: Black Southern music of hard times and humour, built on blue notes and twelve bars.

place.text: African-American communities of the Deep South, especially the Mississippi Delta

description: Blues grew among African Americans in the Deep South, usually dated to the decades after slavery ended, out of work songs, field hollers, spirituals and ballads. Its call-and-response phrasing, blue notes and twelve-bar form run all through jazz, rhythm and blues and rock and roll.
debatable: Where it really began is argued over: some historians trace key elements to the Sahel region of West Africa, others say no single African form is its direct ancestor, and the early years are poorly documented.

listen_for.text: Blue notes: thirds, fifths or sevenths sung or played slightly flat, so the tune sits between happy and sad.
The AAB shape of a verse: a line, the same line again, then a longer answering line.
A shuffle groove with a backbeat, the accent landing on beats two and four.

hallmarks.title: Twelve bars, three chords
hallmarks.text: Most blues runs on a repeating twelve-bar cycle built from three closely related chords. The bars fall into three four-bar phrases that mirror the AAB lyric, with a short 'turnaround' at the end leading back to the top.

hallmarks.title: Call and response
hallmarks.text: Voice and guitar trade lines like a conversation, a habit that goes back to the ring shouts and field hollers sung by enslaved people. Many scholars trace this back-and-forth to African music.

hallmarks.title: Songs of hard times
hallmarks.text: Early blues told loose stories of lost love, police cruelty, segregation and floods, but it could also be funny and saucy. Blues players and gospel singers used the same tools, even as churches called blues the devil's music.

hallmarks.title: The classic blueswomen
hallmarks.text: In the 1920s women singers, many from vaudeville, were the blues' big stars on record. Ma Rainey, the 'Mother of the Blues', and Bessie Smith were two of 'the big three', and some of their records sold to white buyers too.

hallmarks.title: Electric Chicago
hallmarks.text: After the war, migrants from Mississippi plugged in: electric guitar, harmonica through a microphone, bass and drums. Chicago became a centre for this louder sound from 1948, when Muddy Waters had his first hit there, and it later fired up British bands such as the Rolling Stones. B. B. King's string-bending solos went on to shape electric blues guitar.

name: Jazz

tagline.text: New Orleans music of swing and improvising that kept reinventing itself.

place.text: African-American communities of New Orleans, Louisiana

description: Jazz took shape in New Orleans' African-American communities, mixing blues, ragtime, marches, spirituals and dance music, though it did not begin as a single tradition there or anywhere else. Improvising is at its heart, and it changed shape again and again: swing big bands, bebop, cool, modal, free jazz and fusion.
debatable: Jazz is famously hard to define: one writer calls it 'a construct' for many related musics, and Duke Ellington called his own work American Music rather than jazz.

listen_for.text: Swing: instead of splitting each beat evenly, players split it unevenly, in threes over a steady pulse, so the music rolls and bounces.
Solos made up on the spot over the song's chords, often after the tune is stated once.
Instruments talking to each other, from New Orleans players weaving countermelodies around the tune to call and response in the vocals.

hallmarks.title: Swing feel
hallmarks.text: Swing is called the most important African-based rhythmic technique in jazz. Louis Armstrong's oft-quoted line was that if you don't feel it, you'll never know it.

hallmarks.title: Making it up live
hallmarks.text: Improvisation is one of jazz's defining elements, inherited from the blues and work songs. Early New Orleans bands improvised together; later the spotlight moved to the soloist.

hallmarks.title: Big-band swing
hallmarks.text: In the 1930s arranged big bands ruled the dance halls, and star soloists became as famous as the leaders. Ella Fitzgerald rose to fame singing with Chick Webb's band at Harlem's Savoy Ballroom.

hallmarks.title: Bebop's turn
hallmarks.text: In the 1940s bebop players such as Charlie Parker made jazz music for listening, not dancing: faster tempos, trickier chords and racing lines. The response was divided and sometimes hostile, especially from swing players, but by the 1950s bebop was part of the jazz vocabulary.

hallmarks.title: Modes and electricity
hallmarks.text: Miles Davis's Kind of Blue (1959) built solos on scales rather than fast-changing chords, and became the best-selling jazz album. A decade later he went fully electric with In a Silent Way (1969), which can be considered his first fusion album.

name: Gospel music

tagline.text: Christian music of strong voices and harmonies, rooted in Black churches of the South.

place.text: Black churches of the Southern United States, then Chicago

description: Gospel is Christian music led by powerful voices and close harmonies, sung in call and response over clapping and stomping. Black gospel grew from spirituals and hymns in the South, took modern shape in 1930s Chicago, and flowed into soul, rhythm and blues and rock and roll.
debatable: There is no clean founding date: its roots are traced to the early 17th century, the term 'gospel song' first appeared in print in 1874, and 1930 is said to be the year traditional Black gospel began; Thomas Dorsey is often credited with creating it, though he more accurately started a movement that popularised gospel blues.

listen_for.text: Call and response between a lead singer and the choir or congregation.
In older church recordings, hand-clapping and foot-stomping carry the rhythm, often with no band at all.
In singers like Mahalia Jackson: bent, 'worried' blue notes and long runs of several notes on one syllable.

hallmarks.title: Lining out to response
hallmarks.text: One theory traces gospel's call and response to 'lining out', where a leader sang a line and the church sang it back. In Black churches, much singing was a cappella with hands and feet as the drums.

hallmarks.title: Gospel blues
hallmarks.text: Thomas Dorsey, a former blues pianist, saw no real line between blues and church music apart from the words. His songs and his choir conventions spread this gospel blues through Black churches.

hallmarks.title: The great voices
hallmarks.text: Gospel puts the voice first. Mahalia Jackson's huge contralto, improvised phrasing and visible joy carried gospel to concert halls around the world.

hallmarks.title: Sacred meets secular
hallmarks.text: Sister Rosetta Tharpe played electric guitar and took gospel into nightclubs with big bands behind her. Conservative churches objected, but she never left gospel, and her sound fed rock and roll.

hallmarks.title: Urban contemporary
hallmarks.text: From 'Oh Happy Day' in 1969 on, gospel borrowed the rhythms and electronic beats of secular Black music. Later artists like Kirk Franklin made ever bolder moves into the secular world.

name: Country music

tagline.text: Southern ballads and dance tunes on fiddle, banjo and guitar, spread by early radio.

place.text: The American South and the Appalachian Mountains, with Nashville as its radio home

description: Country grew from the folk music of the South and Appalachia, with British folk ballads, cowboy songs, African-American folk songs, spirituals and the blues all in the mix. Radio and records turned 'hillbilly music' into a national genre from the 1920s, and it has reinvented itself every generation since.
debatable: Its roots are both African and European, yet it is now largely linked with white Americans, which has been put down to record labels segregating the music industry from the 1920s.

listen_for.text: Fiddle, banjo, mandolin and steel guitar around a plain, story-telling vocal.
Close family-style harmony singing, as in the Carter Family's mountain gospel sound.
Jimmie Rodgers's 'blue yodel', a yodel set to a steady four-beat time rather than the three-beat alpine kind.

hallmarks.title: Bristol, 1927
hallmarks.text: At the 1927 Bristol sessions, producer Ralph Peer recorded both the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers, a day apart. The two are widely seen as country's important early acts.

hallmarks.title: Radio barn dances
hallmarks.text: Radio grew country's audience in the 1920s. The Grand Ole Opry, broadcast from Nashville since 1925, is still on the air.

hallmarks.title: Honky-tonk
hallmarks.text: A raw sound of guitar, bass and steel guitar grew up in the bar rooms of Texas, Oklahoma and New Mexico, drawing on western swing, Mexican ranchera and the blues of the South. In 1951 Tony Bennett's pop cover of Hank Williams's 'Cold, Cold Heart' took his songwriting to mainstream audiences.

hallmarks.title: Many offshoots
hallmarks.text: In the 1950s and 60s country branched into bluegrass, rockabilly and the polished Nashville sound, with strings and smooth vocals. Outlaw country, from the bars of Oklahoma, New Mexico and Texas, shook things up in the early 1970s with songs of anger and alienation.

hallmarks.title: Crossing over
hallmarks.text: Country singers have often jumped to the pop charts. Dolly Parton's 1977 'Here You Come Again' topped the country chart and reached No. 3 on pop.

name: American folk music revival

tagline.text: Acoustic old songs and new protest songs, sung in coffee houses and at marches.

place.text: New York City, above all Greenwich Village, plus San Francisco's North Beach and college towns

description: The revival brought old American folk songs, and new songs written in their style, to a young city audience from the 1940s to its mid-1960s peak. It was tied to labour and civil rights politics, and it rediscovered forgotten country and blues recordings before rock absorbed it.
debatable: Two scholars speculate that without the anti-communist blacklisting of the 1950s, folk would have hit the mainstream even harder in the early 1950s, perhaps making the 1960s boom redundant.

hallmarks.title: Songs with a cause
hallmarks.text: As a popular movement the revival began with the Weavers, formed by members of People's Songs, a clearing house for union songs. Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie's circle sang about workers, fascism and later civil rights.

hallmarks.title: Blacklist years
hallmarks.text: When Seeger was named as a probable subversive in the Red Scare, the Weavers lost their record deal and radio play. Folk went underground into schools, summer camps and coffee houses.

hallmarks.title: Old records rediscovered
hallmarks.text: Harry Smith's 1952 Anthology of American Folk Music reissued 1920s and 30s country and blues 78s. Young players copied the old singers, and some of those singers, still alive, were brought to the 1963 and 1964 Newport Folk Festivals.

hallmarks.title: Marching songs

name: Punk rock

tagline.text: Short, fast, loud rock stripped to its bones, made by anyone with a guitar.

place.text: The United States (above all New York's CBGB scene), the United Kingdom (London) and Australia (Brisbane and Sydney).

description: Punk rock emerged in the mid-1970s, rooted in 1950s rock and roll and 1960s garage rock, as bands rejected the overproduced, corporate arena rock of the day. Its songs are short and fast, with rough, stripped-down playing and vocals and anti-establishment lyrics, and its do-it-yourself spirit meant self-made records, small labels and small venues. By 1977 it had spread worldwide; in the late 1970s it branched into post-punk and new wave, and in the early 1980s into hardcore.
debatable: The name came before the sound, since critics first used 'punk rock' for 1960s garage bands; and it grew up in several places at once: New York, Ohio, London and Brisbane, where the Saints' Ed Kuepper said they'd been doing this sort of thing for years before hearing the Ramones.

Vocals shouted in a snarl rather than sung, over just guitar, bass and drums.

hallmarks.title: Back to basics

hallmarks.title: Do it yourself
hallmarks.text: Punk prized simple, accessible playing and a do-it-yourself spirit. UK pub rock had built a network of small venues and cheap independent labels, and Australia's Saints self-financed and distributed their own single.

hallmarks.title: Year Zero
hallmarks.text: British punk rejected mainstream rock and its own heroes, and 1976 became a musical and cultural 'Year Zero'. The Sex Pistols' swearing on live TV in December 1976 turned punk into a national media scandal.

hallmarks.title: Blunt, political words

hallmarks.title: A look to shock

name: Alternative rock

tagline.text: Guitar rock from punk's underground: indie labels, college radio, then the 1990s charts.

place.text: The United States and the United Kingdom, in college towns and indie scenes such as Athens, Georgia, Minneapolis, Boston, Manchester and Seattle.

description: Alternative rock grew out of the independent underground that followed punk, made by bands who shared punk's do-it-yourself spirit and kept their distance from mainstream rock and pop. Through the 1980s it lived on small labels, fanzines and college radio, with no single sound beyond a love of guitars. In the 1990s Nirvana's breakthrough and the grunge and Britpop movements carried it into the mainstream.
debatable: 'Alternative' pulls two ways: it can mean music that is fiercely anti-commercial, or simply a music-industry category for what record stores and radio sell, and by 1993 the New York Times said it didn't seem so alternative anymore.

listen_for.text: Guitars that blast power chords, chime with picked riffs, buzz with fuzz and squeal with feedback.
In bands like the Pixies and Nirvana, sudden shifts from quiet verses to loud, heavy choruses.
Lyrics that, more often than in other rock, take on social concerns such as drug use, depression and the environment.

hallmarks.title: Punk's DIY heirs
hallmarks.text: The term first meant musicians shaped by the sound or the independent, do-it-yourself ethos of late-1970s punk. US indie labels like SST and Dischord oversaw the shift from hardcore punk to more varied alternative styles.

hallmarks.title: Life underground
hallmarks.text: In the 1980s alternative bands played small clubs, recorded for indie labels and spread by word of mouth, fanzines and college radio. R.E.M.'s Murmur (1983) was an early success that inspired a wave of jangle pop, built on bright, ringing picked guitar.

hallmarks.title: Two sides of the Atlantic
hallmarks.text: British alternative rock was more pop-minded, more open to dance and club culture, and wrote about British concerns. Writer Simon Reynolds named the Smiths and R.E.M. as the two most important alt-rock bands of the 1980s.

hallmarks.title: Loud-quiet-loud
hallmarks.text: The Pixies built their sound on extreme shifts between dreamy quiet and loud rock, a trick other bands soon copied. Kurt Cobain said that on hearing their Surfer Rosa he felt it had the sound he wanted, and Nirvana used the same quiet-to-loud dynamic.

hallmarks.title: Into the mainstream
hallmarks.text: Nirvana's 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' (1991) set off the grunge boom, and record labels scrambled to sign alternative bands. The 1990s also brought confessional female singer-songwriters like PJ Harvey and Liz Phair, and the women-led Lilith Fair festival.

name: Rhythm and blues

tagline.text: Rocking, beat-heavy Black popular music of the 1940s and 50s that rock and roll grew from.

place.text: African American communities in the United States: its roots in the Deep South, its markets in cities like Chicago, Detroit, New York and Los Angeles, and a key rhythmic thread from New Orleans.

description: Rhythm and blues began in African American communities in the 1940s, when record companies used the name for music sold mainly to Black listeners: rocking, jazz-based music with a heavy, insistent beat. It blended jump blues, big-band swing, gospel, boogie-woogie and blues, played by small bands with piano, guitars, bass, drums and saxophone. In the 1950s white teenagers found it too, and it fed straight into rock and roll, soul and, much later, contemporary R&B.
debatable: The label keeps moving: it began as a record-industry marketing term, Robert Palmer called it a catch-all for music made by and for Black Americans, and Fats Domino insisted that 1950s 'rock 'n' roll' was simply the R&B he had played for years.

listen_for.text: A heavy, insistent beat under swinging, jazz-based playing.
A saxophone alongside piano, one or two guitars, bass and drums, sometimes with backing singers.
Simple repeated parts that mesh into a lilting, often hypnotic groove.

hallmarks.title: Born of migration
hallmarks.text: The great migration of Black Americans to cities like Chicago, Detroit and New York in the 1920s and 1930s created a new market for jazz and blues. Blending those sounds with urban life helped shape rhythm and blues.

hallmarks.title: Jump blues roots
hallmarks.text: Jump blues was a swinging, up-tempo dance mix of jazz, blues and boogie-woogie played by small bands with shouted vocals. Louis Jordan and Big Joe Turner are credited by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with laying R&B's foundation in the 1940s.

hallmarks.title: The New Orleans tinge
hallmarks.text: New Orleans musicians took in Cuban rhythms just as R&B was forming. Producer Dave Bartholomew used a repeating three-note Latin figure (tresillo) on many Fats Domino records, and it became a staple of 1950s rock and roll.

hallmarks.title: Crossing the colour line
hallmarks.text: At first only Black listeners bought R&B records, with no white radio play. In the early 1950s white teenagers began buying them, and Fats Domino's tours brought Black and white youths together, which his biographer links to the breakdown of segregation.

hallmarks.title: Songs of real life
hallmarks.text: R&B lyrics often carry the African American experience of pain and the search for freedom and joy, along with triumphs and failures in the face of racism. Many songs were risqué too, and 'rock and roll' itself had a sexual meaning in R&B before radio softened it.

links.label: rock and roll grew from R&B
links.reason: The immediate roots of rock and roll lay in rhythm and blues, and until about 1957 the two names were used interchangeably.

links.label: soul grew from R&B
links.reason: Soul is rooted in gospel and rhythm and blues, described by AllMusic as R&B made more urban and commercial.

links.label: funk grew from R&B
links.reason: Funk is placed in the lineage of rhythm and blues, jazz and soul, with its rhythmic template in New Orleans R&B.

links.label: reggae drew on R&B
links.reason: Jamaican music developed out of a mix of American R&B and the local mento style on the way to reggae.

links.label: salsa took in R&B
links.reason: Salsa is described as mixing Cuban styles with elements of jazz and R&B.

links.label: modern R&B grew from R&B
links.reason: Contemporary R&B, which developed in the late 1980s, combines rhythm and blues with pop, soul, funk, disco and electronic elements.

name: Soul music

tagline.text: Gospel's fire carried into Black American pop, from church to the charts.

place.text: African-American communities across the United States, with key scenes around labels in Detroit (Motown), Memphis (Stax) and Philadelphia.

description: Soul grew in African-American communities in the late 1950s by bringing the voices and feeling of gospel into rhythm and blues, with touches of jazz. It became tied to the civil rights movement as an expression of Black identity and pride, and in the 1960s it ruled the R&B charts and crossed into pop. Around labels like Motown, Stax and Atlantic it split into many local sounds, and later fed funk, disco and contemporary R&B.
debatable: Who started soul is argued over: Ray Charles is often cited as popularising it, AllMusic's Bruce Eder called Sam Cooke 'the inventor of soul music', and Peter Guralnick dates its start to Solomon Burke's 1961 'Just Out of Reach'.

listen_for.text: Call and response, with the lead singer answered by backing vocalists, as in church.
An especially tense lead voice, with occasional improvised twirls and extra sounds.
Catchy rhythms pushed along by handclaps, with punchy horns and saxophones.

hallmarks.title: Church meets the street
hallmarks.text: Soul came from crossing gospel, the music of Black churches, with secular rhythm and blues, in both words and instruments. Many of its stars started as gospel singers, and moving into secular music could cause controversy.

hallmarks.title: Voice of a movement
hallmarks.text: Soul became linked with the civil rights movement as an expression of Black cultural identity, pride and political awareness. Aretha Franklin's 'Respect' became an anthem for movements for social change.

hallmarks.title: Motown's hit factory
hallmarks.text: Berry Gordy's Motown was notable for being African American owned, and it made hits with an assembly-line approach. Its more rhythmic, pop-friendly sound gave the world the Supremes, the Temptations and Marvin Gaye.

hallmarks.title: The Southern sound
hallmarks.text: Stax in Memphis and Atlantic made dance records with smaller bands, gospel-tinged vocals and lots of brass. Stax often set the voice further back in the mix and let horns do the job of backing singers.

hallmarks.title: Splitting into styles
hallmarks.text: From 1968 soul began to break into subgenres: James Brown and Sly Stone moved into funk, while others made slicker or more political soul. Philadelphia soul brought lush string and horn arrangements, and it is listed among disco's roots.

links.label: soul grew from R&B

links.label: funk emerged from soul
links.reason: James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone moved from soul into funk, and funk vocals keep soul's approach.

links.label: disco grew from soul
links.reason: Philadelphia soul and psychedelic soul are named among disco's roots, and some early-1970s soul records are called a link to disco.

links.label: hip-hop draws on soul
links.reason: Soul is one of the styles hip-hop grew out of.

links.label: Afrobeat took in soul
links.reason: Afrobeat mixes West African music with American funk, jazz and soul influences.

links.label: soul became modern R&B

tagline.text: Black American dance music where the groove of bass, drums and guitar comes first.

place.text: African-American communities in the United States, with deep roots in New Orleans rhythm and blues.

description: Funk grew up in African-American communities in the mid-1960s, mixing the Black popular music of the time into something built for dancing. It turns melody and chord changes down and turns the groove up: an electric bassline and a drum part, often at slower tempos, with every instrument locking into one hypnotic pattern. Its rhythms and breakbeats went on to fuel disco, hip-hop and much of electronic music.
debatable: James Brown is usually named as funk's source, but the Funk article traces its rhythmic template back to New Orleans R&B and Professor Longhair, and Brown himself credited Little Richard's New Orleans road band with first putting the funk into the rhythm.

listen_for.text: A heavy weight on the first beat of each bar, which James Brown called 'The One'.
A bassline that carries the hook, often slapped and popped so it sounds almost like a drum.
Short, muted 'chicken-scratch' guitar chops and gaps between the notes that matter as much as the notes.

hallmarks.title: Everything on The One
hallmarks.text: James Brown shifted his music's weight from the upbeat to the downbeat, leaning hard on the first beat of every bar. Bass, drums and guitar play interlocking, syncopated parts (accents on unexpected beats) that add up to one groove.

hallmarks.title: Room between the notes
hallmarks.text: Funk slowed the tempo down, which left room to split each beat into four quick pulses (sixteenth notes). Its sound depends as much on the rests as on the notes played, giving a beat described as slower, sexier and more syncopated than disco.

hallmarks.title: The bass is the hook
hallmarks.text: Funk has been called the style where the bassline is most prominent, playing the song's catchiest part. Slapping low notes with the thumb and popping high ones with a finger gave the bass a drum-like role.

hallmarks.title: Psychedelic and cosmic
hallmarks.text: From the late 1960s, Sly and the Family Stone and then George Clinton's Parliament-Funkadelic folded in psychedelic rock, with wah pedals, fuzz and echo. Parliament-Funkadelic's Mothership Connection put Black people in outer space, an idea now discussed as Afrofuturism.

hallmarks.title: Songs about Black life
hallmarks.text: Funk lyrics took on the problems faced by Black working-class communities in the 1970s and carried political messages, echoing the civil rights era. Writers note that women in funk, Chaka Khan among them, have been studied far less than the men.

name: Disco

tagline.text: Lush, string-soaked dance music built on a steady kick drum in 1970s clubs.

place.text: Urban nightlife in New York City (especially Brooklyn), Philadelphia and Baltimore, in venues popular with African American, Latino American and Italian American crowds.

description: Disco is dance music that grew out of American city nightlife in the late 1960s, mixing the sounds of venues loved by African American, Latino American and Italian American crowds. Producers working behind the scenes built big, layered records, and DJs learned to mix them into one unbroken night on the dance floor. It filled clubs across the US by the late 1970s, took a sharp backlash in 1979, and lived on in Europe and in the house, techno and hip-hop it helped start.
debatable: Whether disco 'died' is debatable: it fell sharply in the US after Disco Demolition Night in July 1979, but stayed popular in Italy and some other European countries through the 1980s and has had several revivals since the 1990s.

listen_for.text: A kick drum on every beat (four-on-the-floor), with an open, hissing hi-hat landing between the kicks.
A busy, syncopated bassline that often jumps between a note and the same note an octave up.
Strings and horns doubling a soaring, echoey vocal over electric piano and choppy 'chicken-scratch' guitar.

hallmarks.title: Four on the floor
hallmarks.text: The bass drum hits on every beat of the bar, which the Disco article gives as the basic difference between dance music and a rock or pop song. Over it sit fast hi-hats with an open hiss on the off-beat; a mix where drummer Earl Young's hi-hat came out too loud is said to have made loud hi-hats a disco habit.

hallmarks.title: A big, costly sound
hallmarks.text: Disco records often used a large band: several keyboards and guitars, drum kit plus Latin percussion, a horn section and strings. Arrangers, conductors, producers and mixing engineers shaped the result with multitrack recording and effects, and helped create the 'disco sound' itself.

hallmarks.title: The DJ takes charge
hallmarks.text: DJs mixed records with turntables and a mixer into one seamless set, so the dancing never stopped. Tom Moulton found ways to make records longer to keep a crowd moving, and DJs re-edited songs on tape; some, like Larry Levan, also produced records themselves.

hallmarks.title: Machines start to sing
hallmarks.text: Synthesizers crept in, and Donna Summer's 'I Feel Love', produced by Giorgio Moroder in Munich, set repeating synth loops over a constant kick drum and off-beat hi-hat. Writers on techno call it a blueprint for both techno and house about ten years later.

hallmarks.title: A floor to be free on
hallmarks.text: Clubs like the Sanctuary filled with newly liberated gay men at a time when gay sex was illegal in New York state, and writers describe discotheques as spaces where queer people could be themselves. The Paradise Garage, meant for an upscale white gay crowd, instead drew an unlikely mix of Black, Latino and punk dancers from its first nights, and Larry Levan played to them for a decade.

name: Contemporary R&B

tagline.text: Smooth, polished R&B singing over electronic and hip-hop beats, from disco's end on.

place.text: North America, created by African-American musicians.

description: Contemporary R&B is the modern form of rhythm and blues, made by African-American musicians from the end of the disco era onward and folding in pop, funk, soul, jazz, electronic sounds and hip-hop. It is known for its distinctive studio production, lush vocal arrangements and dance or hip-hop beats with the grit smoothed out. From new jack swing in the late 1980s to hip-hop soul, neo soul and electro-R&B, it has kept absorbing the sounds around it.
debatable: Its start date shifts with the source: its own article dates it to the late 1970s and early 1980s, while the Rhythm and blues article says the newer style only took shape in the late 1980s; the line with hip-hop has been blurred ever since.

listen_for.text: Smooth, layered vocal harmonies, with a lead voice that runs one syllable over many notes (melisma).
Programmed, electronic or hip-hop drums under the singing, with the roughness polished off.
A sound built from texture and mood as much as from the song itself.

hallmarks.title: Disco goes electronic
hallmarks.text: The closest forerunner came at the end of the disco era, when Michael Jackson and Quincy Jones added electronic touches for a smoother, dance-floor-friendly style on Off the Wall (1979). Janet Jackson's Control (1986), with producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, fused funk and disco rhythm with synthesizers and a rap sensibility.

hallmarks.title: New jack swing
hallmarks.text: From 1986 Teddy Riley produced R&B with hip-hop rhythms, a blend that was named new jack swing. It brought samples, sound effects and rap sections into R&B production.

hallmarks.title: Hip-hop soul
hallmarks.text: In the 1990s singers met rappers head on: Mary J. Blige's debut is credited with bringing the R&B and hip-hop mix into the mainstream. Lauryn Hill and Missy Elliott blurred the line further by recording both styles.

hallmarks.title: The producer's sound
hallmarks.text: A distinctive record production style is part of the genre's identity. Teddy Riley shaped the late-1980s sound, and in the late 1990s The Neptunes and Timbaland set an influential course for both R&B and hip-hop.

hallmarks.title: Chart dominance and reinvention
hallmarks.text: In the early 2000s R&B and hip-hop dominated the charts, with Usher, Alicia Keys and Beyoncé among the decade's most successful acts. In the 2010s more electronic, machine-made sounds, some EDM-oriented, turned it into electro-R&B, while Latin R&B mixed in trap.

name: Reggae (with ska)

tagline.text: Jamaica's slow, bass-heavy groove, with the guitar chopping on the offbeat.

place.text: Jamaica, especially Kingston; ska took shape in Jamaican studios in the late 1950s

description: Reggae grew out of ska and rocksteady in late-1960s Jamaica, mixing local mento and Rastafarian drumming with American R&B and jazz. It slowed the tempo, let the bass lead, and put short, choppy chords on the offbeat. From the 1970s its sound and its messages of faith and social criticism spread worldwide.
debatable: Where the word came from is unsettled: Toots Hibbert said it simply came out of his mouth while making 'Do the Reggay', historian Steve Barrow credits Clancy Eccles, and Bob Marley said it came from a Spanish term for 'the king's music'.

listen_for.text: A short, scratchy guitar or piano chord on the offbeat, between the counts (the 'skank').
A thick, heavy bass line with the treble turned down, carrying the tune as much as the rhythm.
Drums that lean on the third beat of the bar rather than the first, at a slower pace than ska.

hallmarks.title: Ska, rocksteady, reggae
hallmarks.text: Ska arose in Jamaican studios in the late 1950s from American R&B and mento, with jazzy horns and a walking bass. In the mid-1960s it slowed into rocksteady, and from 1968 rocksteady gave way to reggae. The Wailers are perhaps the best-known band to move through all three stages.

hallmarks.title: The offbeat skank
hallmarks.text: Most pop leans on beat one; reggae accents the offbeats instead. Guitar or piano chops short chords between the counts while the drum stresses beat three, giving it a distinctive sense of phrasing. The intro to the Wailers' 'Stir It Up' is an example of the guitar chop.

hallmarks.title: Bass up front
hallmarks.text: The bass guitar is central, with a thick tone and the high frequencies cut to stress the low end. Drummers stuff the kick drum for a deep, punchy thud and keep time on the hi-hat rather than a ride cymbal.

hallmarks.title: Rastafari and conscious lyrics
hallmarks.text: Reggae is closely tied to Rastafari, an Afrocentric faith that emerged in 1930s Jamaica, and Rasta drummers played on seminal recordings. Lyrics range from love and leisure to social criticism, anti-racism, anti-colonialism and praise of God (Jah).

hallmarks.title: From Kingston to the world
hallmarks.text: Jamaican immigrants in Britain and labels such as Island and Trojan took the music to the UK, where reggae sales exceeded Jamaica's between 1968 and 1972. The 1972 film The Harder They Come, starring Jimmy Cliff, then introduced it to cinema audiences outside Jamaica.

links.label: American R&B roots
links.reason: Ska, reggae's direct ancestor, grew out of Jamaican R&B, which was based largely on American R&B.

links.label: jazz in the horns
links.reason: Reggae's roots in ska and rocksteady were strongly influenced by American jazz, heard in ska's jazz-influenced horn riffs.

links.label: remixed into dub
links.reason: Dub grew out of reggae as engineers stripped reggae tracks back to drums and bass and added echo and reverb.

links.label: via Spanish reggae
links.reason: Reggaeton evolved from dancehall and reggae, starting with the Spanish-language reggae of Panama in the late 1980s.

links.label: a digitised offshoot
links.reason: Jungle, the forerunner of drum and bass, has been called a raved-up, digitised offshoot of Jamaican reggae, and Britain's reggae culture helped form it.

name: Dub

tagline.text: Reggae taken apart at the mixing desk: drum and bass, drenched in echo.

place.text: Jamaica, in Kingston's studios and sound systems

description: Dub is reggae remixed: engineers took existing recordings, pulled out most of the vocals, pushed the drums and bass forward and soaked what was left in delay and reverb. It began with instrumental 'versions' cut for Kingston sound systems and had become its own subgenre by 1973. Its idea of the mixing desk as an instrument fed into post-punk, hip-hop, house, techno, jungle and dubstep.
debatable: No single inventor: a popular origin story is a 1968 dubplate on which an engineer left the vocal out by accident, but the genre article credits several competing engineers and producers, among them King Tubby, Lee Perry and Errol Thompson.

listen_for.text: Vocals and instruments dropping in and out of the mix, leaving sudden gaps.
Long echoes and reverb trailing off a snare hit or a scrap of voice.
A stripped-down drum and bass track (the riddim) pushed right to the front.

hallmarks.title: The B-side version
hallmarks.text: Jamaican singles carried an instrumental 'version' on the B-side, with some or all of the vocal removed, for sound-system deejays to toast (chant or rap) over. Versions were cheap to make from one session and gave engineers room to experiment.

hallmarks.title: The desk as instrument
hallmarks.text: Producers such as King Tubby and Lee Perry treated the mixing console as an instrument. Tubby mixed live, dropping tracks out and bringing them back as the tape ran, on equipment he built and adapted himself.

hallmarks.title: Echo and space
hallmarks.text: Delay units such as the Roland Space Echo, plus reverb and phasing, turn a song into a drifting soundscape. Scholar Michael Veal called dub's reverb a 'sonic metaphor for the condition of diaspora', used to call up memories of African culture.

hallmarks.title: The melodica's voice
hallmarks.text: Augustus Pablo is credited with bringing the melodica, a small keyboard you blow into, into dub. His dub of 'Baby I Love You So', mixed by King Tubby as 'King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown', became one of the most popular dubs of all time.

hallmarks.title: From Kingston to London
hallmarks.text: In the 1970s the UK became a new centre of dub production, with Mad Professor among its best-known names, and punk and post-punk took it up: the Clash worked with Lee Perry and Mikey Dread, and Public Image Ltd used dub-influenced bass lines. Originators like Mad Professor and Lee Perry kept making dub into the 21st century.

name: Salsa

tagline.text: Fast Latin dance music from New York, built on Cuban son and the clave rhythm.

place.text: New York City, among Cuban, Puerto Rican and Dominican musicians

description: Salsa is Caribbean dance music mostly built on Cuban son montuno, with elements of mambo, cha-cha-chá, bolero, rumba, jazz, R&B and Puerto Rican bomba and plena. It took its name and shape in New York in the 1960s and 1970s, where Fania Records gathered Cuban, Puerto Rican and Dominican musicians. From there it spread across Latin America and to Africa.
debatable: The name is contested: the word was pushed as a marketing label, Celia Cruz called salsa Cuban music under another name, and Tito Puente joked that the only salsa he knew was ketchup.

listen_for.text: The clave, a rhythm often struck on two wooden sticks, which the congas, timbales, piano and bongos play with.
A call-and-response section (the montuno) where the lead singer trades lines with a repeated chorus, sometimes speeding up.
Congas, bongos and timbales together, with a piano looping a repeated montuno figure.

hallmarks.title: Cuban son at the core
hallmarks.text: Most salsa rests on the son montuno of 1930s and 1940s Cuban bands such as Arsenio Rodríguez's, who added a horn section and congas to the son ensemble. Many of Arsenio's songs were later covered by salsa bands.

hallmarks.title: The clave rules
hallmarks.text: The clave provides the core groove: congas, timbales, piano and bongos play with it, while bass, maracas and cowbell play independently of it. Most salsa uses the 3-2 or 2-3 son clave.

hallmarks.title: Fania's New York
hallmarks.text: Johnny Pacheco and businessman Jerry Masucci founded Fania Records, which introduced many artists later identified with salsa, including Willie Colón and Celia Cruz. In 1971 the Fania All-Stars sold out Yankee Stadium.

name: Bossa nova

tagline.text: A hushed, swaying samba for nylon-string guitar and soft voice, born in Rio.

place.text: The South Zone of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, with the Copacabana clubs of Beco das Garrafas as its cradle

description: Bossa nova ('new trend') is a relaxed style of samba from late-1950s Rio de Janeiro, in which João Gilberto's guitar distilled a samba band's drumming into a gentle, syncopated pattern. Jobim's rich harmonies and Vinicius de Moraes's lyrics completed the sound, sung softly and close to speech. The 1964 album Getz/Gilberto, a major contributor to its already growing popularity abroad, turned it into a craze in the US and beyond.
debatable: Its debt to jazz is debated: the genre article calls it a misconception that its complex chords came from jazz, since samba guitarists used similar ones from the 1920s, yet says jazz did shape its harmonies and instrumentation.

listen_for.text: A nylon-string guitar played with the fingers: the thumb on the bass like a surdo drum, the fingers on the chords like a tamborim.
A soft, almost spoken voice, recorded at the same level as the guitar.
Unusual, 'ambiguous' chords over a gentle sway that does not swing the way jazz does.

hallmarks.title: Samba on one guitar
hallmarks.text: Gilberto took one layer of a samba percussion section, the tamborim, and moved it into his picking hand, with his thumb standing in for the surdo bass drum. The music keeps samba's stress on the second beat, softened into a swaying motion.

hallmarks.title: The quiet voice
hallmarks.text: Before bossa nova, Brazilian singers used brassy, almost operatic styles. Gilberto sang near the volume of ordinary speech and recorded with two microphones, one for voice and one for guitar, so both carried equally.

hallmarks.title: Jobim's harmonies
hallmarks.text: Antônio Carlos Jobim put sophisticated harmonic structures into popular song, and many of his tunes became jazz standards. 'Garota de Ipanema (The Girl from Ipanema)' is believed to be one of the most recorded popular songs in history.

hallmarks.title: Love, longing, nature
hallmarks.text: Lyrics, many by the poet Vinicius de Moraes, deal with women, love, longing, homesickness and nature. They were often apolitical and pictured middle- and upper-class life, and after the 1964 coup the more political MPB eclipsed bossa nova's popularity.

hallmarks.title: The craze abroad
hallmarks.text: After a 1962 Carnegie Hall concert, Stan Getz recorded Getz/Gilberto with João and Astrud Gilberto and Jobim. Astrud's English vocal on 'The Girl from Ipanema' made it a hit, and the album was the first jazz record to win the Grammy for Album of the Year.

links.label: samba meets cool jazz
links.reason: Bossa nova was influenced by jazz in its harmonies and instrumentation, Jobim is credited with merging samba and cool jazz, and many bossa nova songs are now jazz standards.

name: Afrobeat

tagline.text: Long, chanted Nigerian grooves of highlife, funk and jazz, with a political edge.

place.text: Lagos, Nigeria, where Fela Kuti's club the Afrika Shrine was its home

description: Afrobeat fuses Yoruba music and Ghanaian highlife with American funk, jazz and soul, built from chanted vocals, interlocking rhythms and heavy percussion. Fela Kuti developed it in late-1960s Nigeria with drummer Tony Allen, and used its long, hypnotic songs to attack corruption and military rule. It is not the same as Afrobeats, the 21st-century West African pop sound.
debatable: Afrobeat and Afrobeats are often conflated, but they are different genres: Afrobeats is a 21st-century West African mix of hip-hop, house, jùjú, dancehall and more.

listen_for.text: A long instrumental jam, often 10 to 15 minutes, before the main vocal begins.
Two or more guitars, each repeating one short pattern for the whole song, locking into one groove.
Drums that make sparing use of the usual 2-and-4 backbeat: tightly swung triplets on the hi-hat, and snare patterns that hint at a clave without stating it.

hallmarks.title: Highlife, jazz, then funk
hallmarks.text: Fela studied music in London, where he was exposed to jazz, and first played a highlife-jazz hybrid. He then folded in funk, soul and Yoruba rhythms and vocal traditions; the name Afrobeat was partly meant to set his music apart from American soul artists such as James Brown.

hallmarks.title: Tony Allen's drumming
hallmarks.text: Fela said there would be no Afrobeat without Tony Allen. Allen made sparing use of the plain backbeat, playing tight, swung patterns that imply the clave feel without stating it.

hallmarks.title: Music as protest
hallmarks.text: During a 1969 trip to the US, activist Sandra Smith introduced Fela to Black Power writings, and his songs turned from love to politics. He attacked corruption and military rule, and after his 1977 album Zombie criticised the army, soldiers raided and burned his commune.

hallmarks.title: Long songs, big bands
hallmarks.text: Songs often ran 10 to 30 minutes, opening with an instrumental jam and using call-and-response choruses. Fela's band had two baritone saxophones and two or more guitarists, and he sang mostly in Nigerian Pidgin English so listeners across Africa could follow.

hallmarks.title: A living tradition
hallmarks.text: Fela's sons Femi and Seun carry the style on, and from the late 1990s a small Brooklyn scene grew, with bands such as Antibalas and the Daktaris. Its polyrhythms also reached Western music through Talking Heads' 1980 album Remain in Light.

links.label: soul in the groove

name: Reggaeton

tagline.text: Spanish-language dance music riding the dembow beat, from Panama to Puerto Rico.

place.text: Panama in the late 1980s, then Puerto Rico and Miami from the early 1990s

description: Reggaeton grew from the Spanish-language reggae of Panama, which traces back to Afro-Caribbean workers who came to build the canal, and took shape in Puerto Rico's 'underground' scene of the early 1990s; the name, coined in Puerto Rico, became prominent in the early 2000s. It mixes Jamaican dancehall with hip-hop, rapped or sung in Spanish over the dembow rhythm. Daddy Yankee's 'Gasolina' (2004) opened the door worldwide, and it is now one of the most popular genres in the Spanish-speaking Caribbean.
debatable: Its birthplace is shared: it arose from Panama's Spanish reggae in the late 1980s, but the genre article stresses that its name, technique and consolidation as a genre happened in Puerto Rico.

listen_for.text: The dembow beat: a 3+3+2 pattern (the tresillo) over a steady kick drum in four.
Vocals that move between rapping, singing and rap-singing, usually in Spanish.
A hook repeated through a verse-chorus-bridge structure borrowed from hip-hop.

hallmarks.title: The dembow riddim
hallmarks.text: The core rhythm, dembow, comes from Jamaican dancehall: it is usually credited to producers Steely & Clevie and was first highlighted in Shabba Ranks's 1991 song 'Dem Bow'. Elements of that track, along with Dennis the Menace's 'Pounder (Dub Mix II)', are found in over 80% of reggaeton productions.

hallmarks.title: Underground tapes
hallmarks.text: In early-1990s Puerto Rico, DJs like DJ Playero mixed hip-hop and dancehall on cassettes recorded in carports and public housing, with rappers freestyling in Spanish. The tapes were sold from car trunks and spread among the island's young people.

hallmarks.title: Raids, then acceptance
hallmarks.text: In 1995 Puerto Rican police raided record stores and confiscated 'obscene' underground tapes, and schools banned the music. By 2003 politicians were using reggaeton in election campaigns, and brands later hired Daddy Yankee and Ivy Queen.

hallmarks.title: Afro-Caribbean roots
hallmarks.text: The genre traces back to Panama, where descendants of West Indian canal workers sang reggae in Spanish; El General, of Jamaican descent, grew up in that scene. Its dance, perreo, has roots in Afro-Caribbean dance, and Tego Calderón made Afro-Puerto Rican identity and the discrimination Afro-Latinos face central themes of his music.

hallmarks.title: Breaking a male mould
hallmarks.text: Reggaeton began as a mostly male, macho genre, but Ivy Queen, the 'Queen of Reggaeton', broke through with songs about female empowerment. More recently queer and trans artists have entered the mainstream.

links.reason: Early producers DJ Playero and DJ Nelson were inspired by hip-hop and dancehall, and reggaeton songs follow hip-hop's verse-chorus-bridge structure.

name: Hip-hop

tagline.text: Rhymes over looped breakbeats, born at block parties in the 1970s Bronx.

place.text: The Bronx, New York City, in a multi-ethnic working-class community of African American, Latin American and Caribbean residents.

description: Hip-hop grew up in the early 1970s Bronx, where DJs stretched the instrumental breaks of funk and disco records so dancers and MCs could take over. Rapping became its defining feature, alongside the DJ's turntable tricks like scratching. Over five decades it moved from block parties to the top of the charts, splitting into many regional scenes and styles.
debatable: The date of DJ Kool Herc's August 11, 1973 party has been heavily marketed as the 'Birth of Hip-Hop', and how much the genre owes Jamaica is argued: the article calls dub its strongest artistic precedent, while Herc says his biggest influences were American, above all James Brown.

listen_for.text: A short drum break from an old funk or disco record, looped so it plays over and over.
A rapper (MC) delivering rhythmic, rhyming speech over the beat.
Scratching: the DJ pushing a record back and forth under the needle as an instrument.

hallmarks.title: The break, extended
hallmarks.text: DJs noticed crowds went wild for a record's instrumental break, the short drum-heavy part. DJ Kool Herc used two copies of the same record to stretch it, and Grandmaster Flash and others perfected the trick by cueing breaks precisely.

hallmarks.title: Block party culture
hallmarks.text: Outside the clubs, the biggest incubator was the block party, where DJs hooked sound systems up to street lights. A typical night billed the DJ, the MC and breakdancers, with graffiti artists designing the flyers.

hallmarks.title: The MC steps forward
hallmarks.text: Hip-hop began without rapping as a requirement, but the two became almost the same thing. MCs first introduced the DJ and hyped the crowd, then built call-and-response chants into ever more complex routines; women such as MC Sha-Rock rapped from the start.

hallmarks.title: Machines and samples
hallmarks.text: In the 1980s samplers and drum machines like the Roland TR-808 became affordable, beloved hip-hop tools, and breakbeats no longer needed a DJ and two turntables. Grandmaster Flash's 'Wheels of Steel' (1981) showed the turntable side: a seven-minute collage cut live from other records.

hallmarks.title: Telling it straight
hallmarks.text: 'The Message' (1982), about misery in the housing projects, pioneered politically conscious rap. Golden-age hip-hop, from 1986 to the mid-1990s, carried strong themes of Afrocentrism and political militancy, voiced by acts like Public Enemy and KRS-One; Queen Latifah's 1989 debut made her one of its most notable female rappers.

reacted_against.text: Disco was the dominant sound when hip-hop began, and the article says much of the young genre's early spirit was a rebellion against the disco it came from, even as it inherited disco's studio and DJ techniques.

artists.name: DJ Kool Herc
artists.summary: A Jamaican-American DJ in the Bronx, often called the founder or 'Father of Hip-Hop', who helped popularise the genre from 1973 but made no commercial records in its earliest years.

contributions.text: Playing hard funk records, he isolated the drum break and used two copies on the two-turntable set-up of disco DJs to stretch it, the breakbeat DJing that formed the basis of hip-hop.

He named the dancers b-boys and b-girls and shouted rhyming slang over the music; from 1975 he played the break of the Incredible Bongo Band's 'Apache', which became a b-boy favourite, and his style was taken up by Afrika Bambaataa and Grandmaster Flash.

name: Trap

tagline.text: Southern hip-hop built on booming 808 kicks, rattling hi-hats and dark synths.

place.text: Atlanta, Georgia, and the wider Southern United States

description: Trap is a subgenre of hip-hop from the American South, named after the Atlanta slang for a house where drugs are sold. Its beats are sparse and heavy: deep 808 kick drums, fast-ticking hi-hats and cinematic synthesized strings and brass. In the 2010s it moved from Southern mixtapes to the top of the charts and into pop, R&B and reggaeton.
debatable: Who started it is argued over: T.I. says he coined the term with his 2003 album Trap Muzik, but the genre article names many earlier Southern producers and rappers as pioneers and dates lyrical references to the trap back to 1991.

listen_for.text: Hi-hats ticking in double- and triple-time rolls, much faster than the beat underneath.
Deep 808 kick drums tuned to ring out long, so the kick also hums like a bass note.
Dramatic synthesized strings, brass and keys over a beat that usually runs around 140 beats per minute but feels like a slow 70 (half-time).

hallmarks.title: Music about a place
hallmarks.text: The name comes from Atlanta slang for a drug house, and early trap rappers wrote about life in the trap, drug dealing and the struggle for success. As one critic put it, in the early 2000s the trap was a real place, and the word was later used for music made about that place.

hallmarks.title: The 808 at the centre
hallmarks.text: Trap drums come from the Roland TR-808 drum machine sound: deep kicks, crisp snares and quick hi-hats. Some drums are tuned with a long decay (a slow fade) so they ring out at a bass pitch.

hallmarks.title: Orchestral menace
hallmarks.text: Producers stack synthesized strings, brass and woodwinds over the drums for a cinematic, ominous mood. Shawty Redd's horror-inspired minimalism and DJ Toomp's melodic, sample-based approach set the template, and Lex Luger is often credited with popularising the modern trap sound.

hallmarks.title: Atlanta's pioneers
hallmarks.text: T.I., Jeezy and Gucci Mane are credited together with pioneering trap for mainstream audiences in the 2000s. Their records carried the trap's themes from Southern mixtapes onto national charts and radio.

hallmarks.title: From mixtape to mainstream
hallmarks.text: By the late 2010s trap songs were topping the Billboard Hot 100, and the sound had spread into pop, R&B, K-pop and reggaeton. Cardi B's 'Bodak Yellow' reached number one in 2017, and in 2018 hip-hop became the most popular form of music for the first time, according to Nielsen, as trap rose.

links.label: a Southern hip-hop subgenre
links.reason: Trap is a subgenre of hip-hop from the Southern United States, traced back to gangsta rap.

links.label: trap drums in EDM
links.reason: From 2013 producers such as DJ Snake brought trap-influenced EDM into the mainstream, a fusion known as EDM trap.

name: Synth-pop

tagline.text: Pop songs where synthesizers and drum machines take over from the band.

place.text: Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom; it became a distinct genre in Japan and the UK

description: Synth-pop is pop with the synthesizer in charge, often with drum machines and sequencers standing in for the rest of the band. It arose in Japan and the UK from the late-1970s post-punk and new wave scenes, prefigured by Kraftwerk, and broke through when Gary Numan topped the UK charts in 1979. It went on to directly influence house music and Detroit techno.
debatable: Critics have called it soulless and its players unskilled; OMD's Andy McCluskey answered that real people, not the machines, wrote the songs.

listen_for.text: Simple synth riffs repeated and woven together, often with little chord movement.
A drum machine keeping strict, machine-like time.
In early records, droning electronics and lyrics about isolation and city alienation; in 1980s hits, emotional, sometimes operatic singers and more optimistic songs about romance and escape.

hallmarks.title: Punk picks up a synth
hallmarks.text: Early punk was hostile to the 'inauthentic' synthesizer, but its do-it-yourself attitude let new wave and post-punk bands play one without years of training. Gary Numan found a Minimoog left in the studio and turned Tubeway Army's punk songs into electronic ones.

hallmarks.title: Tokyo's rhythm machine
hallmarks.text: Yellow Magic Orchestra introduced the TR-808 rhythm machine to popular music and developed a breezy, melody-first sound that strongly influenced early British synth-pop. Their early work has also been described as proto-techno.

hallmarks.title: From cold to warm
hallmarks.text: Early synth-pop was minimal and often eerie, with lyrics about isolation and emotional coldness. In the 1980s, dance beats, cheaper polyphonic synths (able to play chords) and MIDI made it warmer and catchier, inside the three-minute pop song.

hallmarks.title: The 1981 peak
hallmarks.text: Synth-pop peaked commercially in the UK in the winter of 1981–82, when the Human League's 'Don't You Want Me' and Soft Cell's 'Tainted Love' were the year's best-selling singles. MTV then carried style-conscious British acts into the US charts.

hallmarks.title: Playing with image
hallmarks.text: Synth-pop stars were often seen as gender-bending, from Phil Oakey's eyeliner to Annie Lennox's early 'dominatrix' image, which tied the genre to alternative sexuality. In the US, critics dismissed such acts as 'English haircut bands'.

links.label: borrowed from disco
links.reason: Synth-pop pursued a deliberate artificiality, drawing on critically derided forms such as disco and glam rock.

links.label: post-punk electronics
links.reason: Synth-pop partly arose from punk rock, as new wave and post-punk bands took up the synthesizer.

links.label: techno-pop into electro
links.reason: Electro grew from funk and boogie mixed with German and Japanese techno-pop, with synth-pop among its roots.

links.label: fed Detroit techno
links.reason: Juan Atkins and others developed Detroit techno from a style influenced by synth-pop and funk.

links.label: an influence on house
links.reason: Synth-pop was a major influence on house music, which grew out of early-1980s post-disco club culture.

name: Electro

tagline.text: Robotic, TR-808-driven funk from early-1980s New York, Detroit and Tokyo.

place.text: New York City (the Bronx), Detroit and Tokyo

description: Electro, also called electro-funk, is dance music built on the Roland TR-808 drum machine, synthetic beats and robotic, vocoder-treated voices. It rose in the early 1980s as disco faded in the US, fusing funk and early hip hop with electronic pop from Germany and Japan. Its machine sound went on to shape Detroit techno, Miami bass, breakbeat and drum and bass.
debatable: The word is slippery: 1980s electro and today's 'electro' dance music both grew out of disco's breakup but are now different genres, and even the definition of an electro beat is called ambiguous.

listen_for.text: The booming kick, sharp handclaps, cowbell and hi-hats of the TR-808 drum machine.
Syncopated, mechanical beats modelled on breakbeats, stiffer than a live drummer.
Voices run through a vocoder or talkbox (devices that make a voice sound robotic or make an instrument 'talk'), robotic chants and science-fiction synth effects.

hallmarks.title: Kraftwerk meets the Bronx
hallmarks.text: Electro joined German and Japanese electronic pop to funk and hip hop. In 1982 Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock', produced by Arthur Baker, rebuilt the synth hook of Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' and drum patterns from their 'Numbers' over TR-808 beats and became a turning point for the genre.

hallmarks.title: The 808 at the centre
hallmarks.text: The TR-808, released in 1980, gave electro its sound: cheap, punchy and with a kick drum that could reach extreme low frequencies. Producers tested tracks in clubs such as New York's Funhouse, where that bass made or broke a record.

hallmarks.title: Space is the place
hallmarks.text: Electro loved science fiction: eerie synth strings, sounds drawn from computer games and cartoons, and lyrics about space and the future, part of an Afrofuturist streak (Black artists imagining the future through technology). Detroit's Cybotron carried the same futurism into what became techno.

hallmarks.title: Rap on the machine
hallmarks.text: Most electro is instrumental, but early electro used rap, and female rappers, from Warp 9 to Roxanne Shante, are part of its tradition. By the mid-1980s rap moved to Run DMC's harder, rock-based beats, and electro's vocal style faded into hip hop.

hallmarks.title: A long afterlife
hallmarks.text: Electro producers such as Arthur Baker went on to Latin freestyle and big pop remixes, while electro fed Detroit techno, breakbeat and drum and bass. The style returned in waves: in the late 1990s, around 2007 and again from 2016.

links.label: technopop meets funk
links.reason: Electro grew from funk and boogie mixed with German and Japanese techno-pop, with synth-pop among its roots.

links.label: funk goes electronic
links.reason: As disco faded, funk acts like Zapp experimented with talk boxes and heavier beats, and electro emerged as a fusion of funk and boogie with German and Japanese technopop.

links.label: rap over drum machines
links.reason: Early electro often used rap, and 'Planet Rock' came out of Bambaataa's Bronx hip-hop scene.

links.label: Detroit electro roots
links.reason: Juan Atkins made electro as Cybotron before techno had its name, and many early British techno producers came to it through electro and hip hop.

links.label: electro in the mix
links.reason: Electro is one of house's roots: early Chicago DJs played electro funk by Afrika Bambaataa and Arthur Baker.

name: Ambient

tagline.text: Music of tone and atmosphere, made to be either ignored or listened to closely.

place.text: Japan and the United Kingdom, with roots in France and Germany

description: Ambient music puts tone, texture and mood ahead of beat or melody, using layers of sound that can sit quietly in the background or reward close listening. It grew in the 1960s and 70s as synthesizers spread, and was named and popularised by Brian Eno with Ambient 1: Music for Airports in 1978. It came back in the late 1980s and 90s through the 'chill-out' rooms of house and techno.
debatable: Eno named it but said others were already making such music, and he later wrote that the term had swollen so much he no longer understood what it stands for.

listen_for.text: Sustained or slowly repeating notes and drones instead of a beat.
Layers of synth texture, sometimes with nature sounds like birdsong or ocean waves.
Music that stays calm at low volume, built to colour a room rather than demand attention.

hallmarks.title: Furniture music
hallmarks.text: In the early 20th century Erik Satie imagined 'furniture music': pieces meant to sit in the background of a dinner, softening the clatter rather than demanding attention. Eno later pointed back to Satie when he named ambient.

hallmarks.title: Synths and systems
hallmarks.text: The arrival of the synthesizer in the 1960s and 70s shaped the genre. Laurie Spiegel made The Expanding Universe on Bell Labs' GROOVE computer system, and German bands such as Tangerine Dream and Kraftwerk were making ambient-style music at the same time.

hallmarks.title: Ignorable and interesting
hallmarks.text: Eno coined the term to set his music apart from canned background music like Muzak. In his notes to Music for Airports he said ambient should allow many levels of attention, be 'as ignorable as it is interesting', and induce calm and a space to think.

hallmarks.title: Letting the system play
hallmarks.text: Eno was drawn to music that runs itself, like overlapping tape loops or wind chimes struck at random by the wind. He called this 'generative music' and named Discreet Music and Music for Airports as early examples.

hallmarks.title: The chill-out room
hallmarks.text: From the late 1980s ambient met rave culture. In 'chill-out rooms' beside the dance floor DJs played ambient, dub and slow beats, and artists like Aphex Twin and The KLF made ambient house and ambient techno as a calm respite from hardcore.

name: House

tagline.text: Chicago's drum-machine dance music, born in Black, Latino and gay clubs.

sources.section: 1980s: Chicago house, acid house and deep house

place.text: Chicago, Illinois, then New York, London, Ibiza and the world

description: House is electronic dance music built on a steady kick drum on every beat, usually at about 120–130 beats per minute. It grew in Chicago in the early-to-mid 1980s, when DJs from the city's queer Black underground clubs began reworking disco records to give them a more mechanical beat; the steady kick may have come from DJs adding drum machines under the records they played. From there it spread to New York, London and Ibiza and became a worldwide sound.
debatable: Nobody agrees where the name came from (the Warehouse club where Frankie Knuckles played, a South Side bar sign, a record-shop bin label or music made at home are all offered), and 'On and On' (1984) is only sometimes called the first house record.

listen_for.text: A four-on-the-floor kick (a bass drum on every beat), claps on beats two and four and off-beat hi-hats, usually from a Roland drum machine.
Deep, bass-heavy loops and samples of disco, soul and funk, built up slowly in repeating eight-bar sections.
Short vocal phrases repeated like a chant, often urging you to 'let yourself go', or no vocals at all.

hallmarks.title: Disco's revenge
hallmarks.text: House picked up where disco left off. After the late-1970s backlash against disco, Chicago DJs stretched and re-edited disco, Philly soul and Euro disco records, adding drum machines and deeper bass. Frankie Knuckles called the result 'disco's revenge'.

hallmarks.title: Warehouse and Music Box
hallmarks.text: Two clubs shaped the sound. At the Warehouse, Frankie Knuckles played smooth, inventive mixes to a mainly Black gay crowd; at its successor, the Music Box, Ron Hardy played louder and wilder, pitching records up and testing brand-new tracks on the dance floor.

hallmarks.title: Tracks made at home
hallmarks.text: After Jesse Saunders's 'On and On' (1984), more and more Chicago DJs released their own tracks on newly cheap drum machines and synths. Phuture bent the squelchy Roland TB-303 bass machine into acid house, and Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body' brought in piano. Labels such as Trax and DJ International carried the records beyond the city.

sources.section: 1980s: Chicago house, acid house and deep house

hallmarks.title: Crossing to Britain
hallmarks.text: Chicago records reached the UK charts from 1986, and Knuckles and Jefferson toured Britain in 1987. By 1988–89 acid house fuelled the rave 'Second Summer of Love', and British house soon found its own voice, built on sample montage, rap and humour.

sources.section: UK: Acid house, rave culture and the Second Summer of Love
1980s: Chicago house, acid house and deep house

hallmarks.title: Church for outsiders
hallmarks.text: Early house spoke to people pushed to the margins, especially African Americans, Latinos and gay clubgoers, who danced together in one of the most integrated spaces of the 1980s. Knuckles called the Warehouse 'church for people who have fallen from grace', and Jefferson compared it to old-time religion.

links.label: disco, re-edited
links.reason: House grew from Chicago DJs re-editing disco records with a more mechanical, repetitive beat and deeper basslines.

name: Techno

tagline.text: Detroit's futuristic machine music, built for long, hypnotic DJ sets.

place.text: Detroit, Michigan, with a second home in Germany (Frankfurt, then Berlin)

description: Techno is repetitive, mostly instrumental electronic dance music made for continuous DJ sets, usually at 120–150 beats per minute. It took shape in and around Detroit in the first half of the 1980s, where young Black producers joined the synthesizers of Kraftwerk and Giorgio Moroder to funk and disco. The name stuck after a 1988 UK compilation, and Berlin became a second centre after the Wall fell.
debatable: There are two origin stories: English-language histories start in 1980s Detroit, while German writing describes techno as a style based on Chicago house that emerged around 1990; the hunt for a 'first techno record' keeps reaching further back.

listen_for.text: A steady four-on-the-floor kick under looping, repeated synth patterns rather than verses and choruses.
In Detroit techno, a basic disco beat often carries extra syncopated, polyrhythmic drum parts (patterns that push against the main pulse); that funkiness sets the Detroit strain apart.
Sound itself as the hook: TR-909 and TR-808 drum machines and synth tones that are slowly filtered and changed.

hallmarks.title: The Belleville Three
hallmarks.text: Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, who met at school in Belleville near Detroit, are seen as techno's first wave. They found common ground between the synthesizers of Kraftwerk, Moroder and Yellow Magic Orchestra and the Black traditions of disco and funk, heard together on The Electrifying Mojo's radio shows.

hallmarks.title: Science-fiction soul
hallmarks.text: The Detroit producers were inspired by science fiction and futurology; Atkins took the word 'techno' from Alvin Toffler's writing. May described the music as George Clinton and Kraftwerk stuck in an elevator with only a sequencer for company.

hallmarks.title: Naming the sound
hallmarks.text: Atkins's records, from Cybotron's 'Alleys of Your Mind' (1981) to Model 500's 'No UFO's' (1985), mapped out the sound. In 1988 the UK compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, first planned as The House Sound of Detroit, fixed the name.

hallmarks.title: The second wave

hallmarks.title: Berlin and beyond
hallmarks.text: Techno became a mass movement in Germany after the first Love Parade in 1989 and the opening of clubs such as Tresor in former East Berlin. Berlin forged close links with Detroit, and artists such as Atkins and Mills played and recorded there.

name: Trance

tagline.text: Hypnotic Frankfurt-born dance music of long builds, breakdowns and peaks.

place.text: Frankfurt, Germany, then across Western Europe

description: Trance is electronic dance music of repeating melodic phrases that build tension through a track towards one or two big peaks, usually at 120–150 beats per minute. It emerged from Frankfurt's techno and EBM (electronic body music) scene in the late 1980s and early 1990s and spread quickly through Europe. Its name comes from the hypnotic, trance-like state the music set out to create.
debatable: Who named and started it is argued: Frankfurt DJ Dag Lerner says he was first to call his music trance, while a claim that it began with Paul van Dyk's 1993 'Love Stimulation' remix has little evidence behind it.

listen_for.text: A long build to a climax, then a soft breakdown where the beat drops away and the melody floats alone before it builds again.
One central melodic hook, rapid arpeggios (a chord's notes played quickly in turn) and minor keys.
A four-on-the-floor kick that sits back to leave room for the bassline; in more recent trance, long snare rolls often build into the big transitions.

hallmarks.title: The Frankfurt sound
hallmarks.text: Early trance was defined by Frankfurt's labels and clubs. Sven Väth, inspired by trance-inducing beach parties in Goa, shaped the music at the Omen club and launched the labels Eye Q (1991), the softer side, and Harthouse (1992), the harder.

hallmarks.title: Berlin's MFS
hallmarks.text: In Berlin, MFS Records signed Paul van Dyk and released early classics such as Humate's 'Love Stimulation' and perhaps the first trance compilation. Van Dyk's Visions of Shiva project with Cosmic Baby brought him into the heart of the scene.

hallmarks.title: Build, break, release
hallmarks.text: Trance is built in blocks of 4, 8, 16 or 32 bars, with instruments added and taken away. Before the breakdown the lead melody is teased in a sliced-up form; afterwards the climax brings the full theme back.

hallmarks.title: Dream trance
hallmarks.text: In the mid-1990s Robert Miles led dream trance with 'Children', a piano-led piece he wrote partly to calm ravers before they drove home from parties.

hallmarks.title: Uplifting and worldwide
hallmarks.text: By the late 1990s uplifting trance took over, with fast tempos, long breakdowns and big drops, and trance was arguably at its commercial peak in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Radio shows such as Armin van Buuren's A State of Trance carried it round the world.

name: Drum and bass (with jungle)

tagline.text: Fast UK breakbeats over deep sub-bass, grown out of the jungle scene.

place.text: United Kingdom, especially London and Bristol

description: Drum and bass is fast electronic dance music, typically 165–185 beats per minute, built on chopped-up breakbeats (drum breaks sampled from old records) over heavy bass and sub-bass. It grew from the UK jungle scene of the early 1990s, which joined rave's breakbeat hardcore to Jamaican sound-system culture: reggae, dub and dancehall. By the mid-1990s it had become one of the most technically inventive styles in dance music.
debatable: Jungle and drum and bass overlap and the line between them is disputed; writers describe a false split in the late 1990s that cast drum and bass as music for white ravers and jungle for Black ravers.

listen_for.text: Rapid, heavily edited breakbeats, very often the 'Amen break', a drum solo sampled from The Winstons' 'Amen Brother'.
A deep sub-bass line you feel in your body as much as hear.
The 'drop': after a build and a breakdown the beats crash back in, more complex and with a heavier bassline, sometimes with an MC hyping the crowd.

hallmarks.title: Sound-system roots
hallmarks.text: Through Britain's African-Caribbean sound-system scene, Jamaican dub and reggae gave jungle its bass weight, with ragga vocals (Jamaican dancehall-style chanting) and MC chants on top. Simon Reynolds called jungle Britain's own answer to hip hop and a digitised offshoot of reggae.

hallmarks.title: Pirate radio and raves
hallmarks.text: The sound was championed at London clubs and on pirate stations such as Kool FM by DJs including Fabio & Grooverider and DJ Rap, before legal radio caught on from 1994 with shows on Kiss 100 and BBC Radio 1.

hallmarks.title: Timeless
hallmarks.text: Goldie's 1995 album Timeless, which set jungle's breakbeats and basslines against orchestral textures and soul vocals, was among the first mainstream drum and bass releases and helped popularise the sound.

hallmarks.title: The light side
hallmarks.text: LTJ Bukem and his Good Looking label led a jazzy, atmospheric strand that came to be called intelligent drum and bass, drawing on 1970s jazz fusion and Detroit techno. It sits opposite the 'heavy', sci-fi-influenced styles like techstep.

hallmarks.title: Live and acclaimed
hallmarks.text: In Bristol, Roni Size's Reprazent took the music on stage with live drums and double bass, and their album New Forms won the 1997 Mercury Prize. The genre has kept renewing itself, with a strong revival among young listeners in the 2020s.

artists.name: Goldie
artists.summary: An English producer, DJ, graffiti artist and actor known for his pioneering role in 1990s jungle and drum and bass, and co-founder of the Metalheadz label.

name: UK garage

tagline.text: London's shuffling, soulful 130 bpm sound of chopped vocals and 2-step beats.

place.text: London, England, then clubs across the UK

description: UK garage is London dance music of shuffled, syncopated drums, deep bass and chopped-up, pitch-shifted vocal samples, usually around 130 beats per minute. It grew in the early-to-mid 1990s from New York garage house played faster in the second rooms of jungle nights, mixed with jungle, ragga, dancehall, gospel and R&B. Its 2-step form became a fixture of the UK charts around 1999–2001 before feeding grime and dubstep.

hallmarks.title: Speeding up New York
hallmarks.text: In 1994 DJ EZ played Todd Edwards' garage house track 'The Praise' at about 130 beats per minute instead of the American 120, closer to the tempo of jungle. Played this way, the US sound became speed garage.

hallmarks.title: Vocals as instruments
hallmarks.text: Todd Edwards cut vocals into tiny fragments and replayed them like percussion instead of using whole verses and choruses. His chopped-sample style became an early mark of speed garage and then 2-step.

hallmarks.title: The Sunday scene
hallmarks.text: Garage first grew on Sundays, partly because jungle held Friday and Saturday nights, and its slower, more sensual 130 bpm drew dancers, many of them women, away from harsher jungle. Pirate radio spread it, from London Underground to So Solid Crew's 'So Solid Sundays'.

hallmarks.title: 2-step takes the charts
hallmarks.text: From about 1998, 2-step's R&B vocals and broken beats went mainstream. MJ Cole's 'Sincere', Artful Dodger's 'Re-Rewind' with Craig David, and David's number one 'Fill Me In' made garage a fixture of the UK chart.

hallmarks.title: MCs and the road to grime
hallmarks.text: The MC, rooted in the Jamaican dancehall tradition of 'toasting' (talking or chanting over a record to work up the crowd), became central to garage. So Solid Crew's darker, MC-led sound took '21 Seconds' to number one in 2001 and pointed the way to grime.

name: Dubstep

tagline.text: Dark, spacious South London bass music at 140 bpm, born from UK garage.

place.text: South London (Croydon and Brixton), England

description: Dubstep is sparse, dark electronic music built on syncopated rhythms and huge sub-bass, almost always around 140 beats per minute. It emerged in South London in the early 2000s as an offshoot of UK garage, blending 2-step rhythms with dub's spacious production and touches of drum and bass and grime. A harsher American offshoot, brostep, later made it a US festival sound.
debatable: The name has more than one claimed origin (Neil Jolliffe of Tempa is said to have coined it in 2002, but 'dub step' was in use by 2001), and some use 'brostep' as a put-down for the louder American style.

listen_for.text: A clap or snare usually on the third beat of each bar at about 140 bpm, with tracks so empty that, as Kode9 put it, you 'almost fill in the double time yourself'.
Prominent sub-bass and, in some strands, the 'wobble': a long bass note made to pulse rhythmically.
Lots of empty space and minor keys, with the bass dropping in hard after a pause.

hallmarks.title: Big Apple and FWD>>
hallmarks.text: Croydon's Big Apple record shop and the FWD>> club night, founded in 2001 and later held at Plastic People, were where the sound took shape. Skream worked in the shop as a teenager and Benga was a regular there.

hallmarks.title: Sound-system thinking
hallmarks.text: Digital Mystikz (Mala and Coki), with Loefah and MC Sgt Pokes, brought sound-system thinking, dub values and jungle's bass weight, and DMZ fliers told dancers to 'come meditate on bass weight'. A 600-person queue at the DMZ night's first anniversary in Brixton is seen as a pivotal moment.

hallmarks.title: Radio takes it worldwide
hallmarks.text: John Peel played dubstep from 2003, and Mary Anne Hobbs's 2006 'Dubstep Warz' show on BBC Radio 1 gave a UK underground scene a global audience.

hallmarks.title: Melody and ghosts
hallmarks.text: Skream's 'Midnight Request Line' (2005) pushed dubstep towards melody and crossed over. Burial's albums, full of vinyl crackle, rain and pitch-shifted voices, took its dark mood somewhere emotional and haunted.

hallmarks.title: Brostep and after
hallmarks.text: Around 2010–11 dubstep reached the pop charts, and in the US a harsher, metal-edged style called brostep made it a mass sound, swapping deep sub-bass for mid-range riffs. Some UK pioneers moved on: Skream to house and techno, Loefah to UK bass.

name: EDM (2010s boom)

tagline.text: The 2010s US festival boom of drop-heavy, stadium-sized dance music.

place.text: United States, led by DJs from Europe and North America

description: 'EDM', short for electronic dance music, is an old umbrella name that the American music industry pushed in the late 2000s and early 2010s to rebrand US rave culture. The boom it labelled was a big-stage, drop-heavy sound somewhere between electro and progressive house, played by celebrity DJs at festivals such as Electric Daisy Carnival and Ultra. It made dance music central to US pop until the boom levelled off in the late 2010s.
debatable: Is it a genre at all? The industry treated 'EDM' as a brand, but the name is still used as an umbrella for many older genres, and in the UK people tend to just say 'dance music'.

listen_for.text: A long build that pauses, then explodes into 'the drop', made for festival crowds.
Big electro and progressive house synths at around 128 beats per minute, often with pop vocals on top.
In its dubstep-influenced strand, harsh 'brostep' bass riffs compared to heavy metal.

hallmarks.title: A rebrand for rave
hallmarks.text: Electronic dance music was already a wide family of genres when, by the early 2010s, the US industry and music press began pushing 'EDM' as a fresh label for American rave culture, setting it apart from 1990s raves.

hallmarks.title: Pop crossovers
hallmarks.text: From 2009 David Guetta scored regular crossover hits with pop and hip-hop stars, such as 'When Love Takes Over' with Kelly Rowland. Avicii later blended house with folk and country on 'Wake Me Up'.

hallmarks.title: Festivals and stadiums
hallmarks.text: Festivals such as Electric Daisy Carnival and Ultra grew huge, with DJs as celebrities and big visual shows. In December 2011 Swedish House Mafia became the first electronic act to sell out New York's Madison Square Garden.

hallmarks.title: The brostep strand
hallmarks.text: Skrillex popularised a harsher dubstep sound called brostep, compared to heavy metal in its aggression. In 2011 Spin hailed a 'new rave generation' led by Guetta, Deadmau5 and Skrillex.

hallmarks.title: Big business, and backlash
hallmarks.text: From 2012 corporations bought up festivals and promoters, and brands used EDM to reach young people. Veteran DJs criticised 'press-play' sets, Deadmau5 said popular EDM 'all sounds the same', Avicii said most of it lacked longevity, and by the late 2010s the boom had plateaued.
